title: 2 Kings 17:24–41
context: The Assyrian king resettles the cities of Samaria with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim. After an attack by lions, an exiled Israelite priest is sent to teach them to fear the LORD, but each group keeps its own gods alongside him. In 17:27 the WEB reads let him go and dwell there, while the traditional Hebrew has them; the singular fits the one priest named in the verse, and why the Hebrew has the plural is not certain. Ezra 4:2 and 4:10 mention later settlements as well, so the population may have been formed in more than one wave.

verses.text: The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, from Cuthah, from Avva, and from Hamath and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel; and they possessed Samaria and lived in its cities.
verses.arminianNotes: The Assyrian king settles foreign peoples in Samaria’s cities. Arminian readers note the human tragedy of population transfers, which uprooted many peoples, not only Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the land given to Israel is now occupied by others, a vivid sign of covenant loss. Ezra 4:2 and 4:10 suggest that settlement may have continued under later kings.

verses.text: So it was, at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they didn’t fear the LORD. Therefore the LORD sent lions among them, which killed some of them.
verses.arminianNotes: At first the settlers did not fear the LORD, and lions killed some of them. Arminian readers see God’s concern for his land and his name even among those who did not know him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God asserting his ownership of the land even after Israel’s removal. Lions appear elsewhere in Kings as instruments of judgment (1 Kings 13:24; 20:36).

verses.text: Therefore they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The nations which you have carried away and placed in the cities of Samaria don’t know the law of the god of the land. Therefore he has sent lions among them; and behold, they kill them, because they don’t know the law of the god of the land.”
verses.arminianNotes: The settlers report that they do not know the law of the god of the land. Arminian readers note their sincere but limited understanding, treating the LORD as a local deity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the settlers interpret events through a territorial view of gods, while the narrator has shown that the LORD is God of all the earth. Their response is religious but misinformed.

verses.text: Then the king of Assyria commanded, saying, “Carry there one of the priests whom you brought from there; and let him go and dwell there, and let him teach them the law of the god of the land.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Assyrian king orders one of the exiled priests to be sent back to instruct the settlers. Arminian readers see a practical attempt to stop the lions, not a turning of the heart, yet God allows even this to bring the newcomers some knowledge of himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the remedy comes from a pagan king for pragmatic reasons, and that the priest chosen was one of those carried away from Samaria, presumably tied to the northern worship Israel had been judged for. God’s truth reaches the settlers through flawed channels.

verses.text: So one of the priests whom they had carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and taught them how they should fear the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The priest settles at Bethel and teaches them how to fear the LORD. Arminian readers note that some instruction in the true God reached the newcomers, giving them a real opportunity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Bethel was the site of Jeroboam’s calf shrine (1 Kings 12:29), so the teaching came from a compromised center of worship.

verses.text: However every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities in which they lived.
verses.arminianNotes: Each nation made its own gods and placed them in the high places the Samaritans had built. Arminian readers see syncretism as a choice to keep old loyalties while adding a new one.
verses.reformedNotes: Samaritans here means the people of Samaria; how this group relates to the later Samaritan community is debated. Reformed readers see mixed worship as no true worship at all.

verses.text: The men of Babylon made Succoth Benoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima,
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Babylon made Succoth Benoth, the men of Cuth Nergal, and the men of Hamath Ashima. Arminian readers note that each group kept the deities of its homeland.
verses.reformedNotes: Nergal is known as a Mesopotamian deity, while the identities of Succoth Benoth and Ashima are less certain. Reformed readers see in the list the many gods that competed with the LORD in the land.

verses.text: and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
verses.arminianNotes: The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their children to Adrammelech and Anammelech. Arminian readers state clearly that child sacrifice continued, a grave evil the text names without softening.
verses.reformedNotes: The identities of these deities are uncertain. Reformed readers note that the settlers repeated the very sin listed in Israel’s indictment (17:17), so the land remained defiled.

verses.text: So they feared the LORD, and also made from among themselves priests of the high places for themselves, who sacrificed for them in the houses of the high places.
verses.arminianNotes: They feared the LORD and also appointed their own priests for the high places. Arminian readers see a divided loyalty that adds the LORD to other gods rather than turning wholly to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the fear of the LORD here is outward and partial. Appointing priests from among themselves echoes Jeroboam’s practice (1 Kings 12:31).

verses.text: They feared the LORD, and also served their own gods, after the ways of the nations from among whom they had been carried away.
verses.arminianNotes: They feared the LORD and served their own gods. Arminian readers stress that God does not accept a share of devotion alongside idols; he calls for the whole heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a summary of syncretism: worship of the true God mixed with false gods, after the customs of their former lands.

verses.text: To this day they do what they did before. They don’t fear the LORD, and they do not follow the statutes, or the ordinances, or the law, or the commandment which the LORD commanded the children of Jacob, whom he named Israel;
verses.arminianNotes: To this day they do not fear the LORD or follow his law. Arminian readers note the apparent contradiction with 17:33 and read it as distinguishing outward reverence from covenant obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see that true fear of the LORD means keeping his covenant, which the settlers did not do. Outward ritual does not count as fearing God.

verses.text: with whom the LORD had made a covenant and commanded them, saying, “You shall not fear other gods, nor bow yourselves to them, nor serve them, nor sacrifice to them;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD had made a covenant forbidding Israel to fear other gods. Arminian readers note that the covenant was clear and offered in love, calling for exclusive loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant restated to show the standard both Israel and the settlers failed. The four verbs forbid every form of devotion to other gods.

verses.text: but you shall fear the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt with great power and with an outstretched arm, and you shall bow yourselves to him, and you shall sacrifice to him.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel was to fear the LORD who brought them out of Egypt with power. Arminian readers see grace preceding command, with God’s redemption as the reason for loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the exodus grounds the command. The outstretched arm recalls God’s mighty acts, which should have secured Israel’s gratitude and undivided worship.

verses.text: The statutes and the ordinances, and the law and the commandment which he wrote for you, you shall observe to do forever more. You shall not fear other gods.
verses.arminianNotes: The statutes, ordinances, law, and commandment God wrote were to be kept forever. Arminian readers stress that covenant obedience was meant to be lasting and wholehearted, not occasional or mixed with other loyalties.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reference to what God himself wrote, recalling the tablets of the covenant. The repeated command not to fear other gods marks exclusive loyalty as the heart of the law.

verses.text: You shall not forget the covenant that I have made with you. You shall not fear other gods.
verses.arminianNotes: The charge not to forget the covenant follows. Arminian readers see memory as an active discipline: forgetting God’s covenant was the first step toward the idolatry the chapter describes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the refrain against fearing other gods is now repeated a third time in this short speech, a deliberate emphasis on the single demand Israel and the settlers alike failed to keep.

verses.text: But you shall fear the LORD your God, and he will deliver you out of the hand of all your enemies.”
verses.arminianNotes: The positive command comes with a promise of deliverance from enemies. Arminian readers see a genuine promise attached to a genuine call, and they note how different Israel’s story might have been had they heeded it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see deliverance as the gracious promise God attaches to the fear of his name. The verse sets the lost alternative beside the exile just described, showing that judgment was never God’s only word.

verses.text: However they didn’t listen, but they did what they did before.
verses.arminianNotes: The settlers did not listen but kept to their former ways. Arminian readers see the settlers repeating Israel’s refusal, as if the land’s history were being replayed by new inhabitants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same verdict given on Israel in 17:14 now falls on the settlers. Without a changed heart, a change of population does not produce a change of worship.

verses.text: So these nations feared the LORD, and also served their engraved images. Their children did likewise, and so did their children’s children. They do as their fathers did to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: These nations combined reverence for the LORD with their engraved images, and their children and grandchildren did the same. Arminian readers see how compromise is passed down, shaping later generations who receive it as normal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the chapter closing on a sober note: syncretism continues to the narrator’s day. The land awaits a renewal that only God can bring, a hope the prophets later announce.
